subject: Biotechnology
title: Expression Systems
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Expression Systems.

hook.text: Getting a gene into a cell is not enough — it must be expressed. The cell has to read and build the protein.

buildup.text: Promoters control when and how much protein is made — strong promoters drive high-volume production.

discovery.text: Inducible promoters let you switch expression on with a chemical — production only when you want it.

twist.text: Codon optimization rewrites the gene in the host's preferred dialect — same protein, different spelling.

climax.text: E. coli, yeast, insect cells, and CHO cells each offer trade-offs — speed versus folding versus glycosylation.

punchline.text: Insert the gene, choose the host, tune the expression — engineering at every step.

quiz.question: What is codon optimization?
options: Removing unnecessary codons to make proteins shorter
Rewriting a gene using the host organism's preferred codons to boost expression
Adding extra stop codons to prevent protein overproduction

details.summary: Expression systems are biological platforms, including bacteria, yeast, insect cells, and mammalian cells, used to produce recombinant proteins at scale. Each system offers different advantages in speed, cost, protein complexity, and post-translational modifications for specific applications.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing the right expression system determines whether a recombinant protein is functional, safe, and economical to produce. The decision between E.
takeaways: E. coli offers fastest and cheapest protein production but limited modifications
Mammalian cells provide human-like modifications essential for therapeutic antibodies
Insect cell baculovirus systems balance complexity and cost for many proteins

faq.question: Why not always use the cheapest expression system?
faq.answer: E. coli is cheapest but cannot add sugar modifications or fold complex multi-domain proteins correctly. Therapeutic antibodies require mammalian cells for proper glycosylation essential to function and safety. Each protein's complexity dictates the minimum expression system sophistication needed.

faq.question: What determines which expression system to use for a new protein?
faq.answer: Key factors include whether the protein needs glycosylation, disulfide bonds, or other modifications; required production scale and cost; regulatory precedent for the therapeutic application; and protein complexity. Simple industrial enzymes use bacteria; complex therapeutics use mammalian cells.
